body: In 2012, Airbus discovered cracks in the wing rib feet of the A380. The rib feet are structural components inside the wing that connect the internal ribs to the wing skin panels. Nearly 80 A380s were in service at the time, and cracks were found on around 40 aircraft, roughly half the active fleet; according to BBC reports at the time, aircraft operated by Air France, Emirates, and Singapore Airlines were among those affected. The investigation linked the cracking to the combination of aluminum alloy rib feet and carbon-composite brackets, together with stresses introduced during manufacturing. The European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) required inspections across the fleet and warned that the issue, if not detected and corrected, could potentially affect the structural integrity of the aircraft.

The composite brackets had been a weight-saving measure, saving around 660 lb (299 kg) per wing. Later in 2012, Airbus introduced a redesigned wing rib foot assembly that replaced the carbon-composite brackets with conventional aluminum components, a solution already proven on other Airbus aircraft. The fleet was not grounded: Airbus worked with EASA to keep the A380 in service under the regulator's airworthiness directive while the permanent fix was developed, certified, and introduced. The retrofit program began in late 2012, covered approximately 120 aircraft, and reportedly cost around $330 million. From 2014 onwards, newly built A380s were delivered with the updated wing structure as the production standard.

Later cracking findings involved different parts of the wing and were not related to the 2012 issue. In 2019, tiny cracks were identified around the outer rear wing spar on a number of early-production A380s, and a total of 25 aircraft required inspections; EASA described the issue as "relatively minor cracking", and inspections could generally be completed during scheduled heavy maintenance checks. By 2024, the regulator had expanded the inspection program to cover all A380 aircraft and additional areas of the wing, and introduced criteria based on how long an aircraft had spent parked or in storage, after data showed a clear link between time on the ground and the severity of the cracks.

In 2026, EASA issued emergency airworthiness directive 2026-0119-E, requiring urgent inspections of the wing mid-spars on 16 A380s: 15 operated by Emirates and one Qantas aircraft, VH-OQI. Five of the Emirates aircraft had to be inspected before further flight, while the remaining aircraft were given a compliance period of 25 flight cycles. The Qantas aircraft was already undergoing heavy maintenance in Dresden, Germany, and the airline told The Guardian the directive had no impact on its flight schedule. Despite the recurring directives, more than 100 A380s remain in service, and according to Cirium, airlines have scheduled more than 83,000 flights using the A380 in 2026.
en.summary: Cracks found in A380 wing rib feet in 2012 affected about half the active fleet. Airbus switched back to aluminum brackets and retrofitted the fleet under an EASA directive, while later, unrelated wing inspections have continued.
en.title: How Airbus fixed the A380's wing cracks without grounding the fleet

facts.claim: In 2012, cracks were discovered in the A380's wing rib feet, affecting around 40 of the nearly 80 A380s then in service.
The cracking was linked to aluminum alloy rib feet combined with carbon-composite brackets and stresses introduced during manufacturing; EASA required fleet inspections.

In late 2012 Airbus introduced a redesigned rib foot assembly with aluminum brackets; the retrofit covered approximately 120 aircraft at a reported cost of around $330 million, and the updated structure became the production standard from 2014.
In 2019, tiny cracks around the outer rear wing spar on early-production A380s led to inspections of 25 aircraft, described by EASA as relatively minor cracking.

EASA emergency airworthiness directive 2026-0119-E required urgent wing mid-spar inspections on 16 A380s (15 Emirates, one Qantas VH-OQI), with five Emirates aircraft inspected before further flight and the rest given 25 flight cycles.
More than 100 A380s remain in service, and Cirium data cited by Simple Flying shows airlines scheduled more than 83,000 A380 flights in 2026.

body: 2012年，空中巴士在A380的機翼肋腳發現裂紋。肋腳是機翼內部連接翼肋與蒙皮的結構件，當時全球約有80架A380在服役，其中約40架發現裂紋，相當於近半數機隊；據BBC當時報導，法國航空、阿聯酋航空與新加坡航空的飛機也在名單之中。調查認定，肋腳使用的鋁合金與其支架使用的碳纖維複合材料並用，加上製造過程引入的應力，使裂紋隨時間形成。歐洲航空安全局（EASA）隨後發布適航指令要求全機隊檢查，並警告此問題若未發現與改正，可能影響飛機的結構完整性。

複合材料支架原本是減重設計的一環，每側機翼可省下約660磅（299公斤）。空中巴士在2012年稍晚推出重新設計的肋腳組件，把複合材料支架換回其他機型早已驗證的傳統鋁合金件。機隊並未因此停飛：空中巴士與EASA合作，讓A380在適航指令的檢查規範下繼續營運，同時開發、認證並導入永久修正。改裝計畫於2012年底展開，涵蓋約120架飛機，據報導耗資約3.3億美元；2014年起出廠的A380直接以新結構為生產標準。
其後發現的裂紋與2012年並非同一問題。2019年，早期出廠的A380在外側後翼樑附近發現細小裂紋，共25架需要檢查，EASA當時形容為「relatively minor cracking」，檢查多可在定期重維修時完成，對營運影響有限。2024年，EASA把檢查擴大到全數A380與更多翼樑區域，並把飛機停放與封存的時間納入檢查時機的判斷，因為資料顯示地面停放時間與裂紋嚴重程度有關。

最新一波是2026年的緊急適航指令2026-0119-E，針對16架A380的機翼中翼樑要求緊急檢查，其中15架屬阿聯酋航空、1架為澳洲航空的VH-OQI；阿聯酋航空其中5架須在下一次飛行前完成檢查，其餘給予25個飛行循環的期限。澳航該架飛機當時已在德國德勒斯登進行重維修，澳航向《衛報》表示對航班時刻表沒有影響。儘管檢查指令多年來從未間斷，A380至今仍有100多架在役，據Cirium統計，航空公司在2026年為A380排了超過8.3萬個航班。
zh.summary: 2012年A380機翼肋腳發現裂紋、約半數服役機隊受影響。空中巴士改採鋁合金組件並配合EASA指令分階段改裝，機隊未停飛；其後不同部位的裂紋檢查則延續至今。
zh.title: A380機翼裂紋當年如何化解：空中巴士換掉複合材料支架、讓機隊免於停飛
